newsitem.title: USA: Scientists discover first nematode-resistant gene.
newsitem.headline: Scientists discover first nematode-resistant gene.

text.p: Plant breeders in Europe have discovered the first gene known to be resistant to nematodes, according to an article in this week's "Science" journal.

Plant breeder Christian Jung of the Institute of Crop Science and Plant Breeding at the University of Kiel in Germany and his colleagues in Denmark and the Netherlands successfully cloned a nematode-resistant gene from a wild beet plant. The gene can be transferred into sugar beets where it has been found to provide the same protection.
Nematodes are microsopic worms that destroy about $100 billion worth of crops worldwide every year.
The nematode in sugar beets can be especially difficult to fight, since the worm can survive in the soil for up to ten years and attacts the plant's roots.
Classical plant breeding has so far failed to produce crops resistant to nematodes, so producers generally rely on pesticides and crop rotation to protect from an onslaught.

Although researches have identified in recent years more than a dozen genes that make plants resistant to pathogens including bacteria, viruses and fungi, this is the first one found to be resistant to an animal pest.
Scientists said that isolating the gene "offers the possibility of transferring resistance to other agriculturally significant species," such as rapeseed.
Researchers said that nematodes trying to feed on the resistant roots were thwarted when their feed structures degenerated, but said they are still unclear about what causes that degeneration.
